themes.label: Exams and grading
themes.selection: Check the current exam formats and assessment weights, and consider how the exam schedule fits with your other courses.
themes.study: Confirm the exam scope and format early. Practise under timed conditions and focus on understanding rather than memorising answers.

evidence.quote: The course is the easiest COMP course I have ever taken, so you can get a very high score if your are careful enough in your exam and homework.

themes.label: Assignments and projects
themes.selection: Map assignments and projects across the semester before combining this course with other demanding courses.
themes.study: Break each task into milestones, prepare an early draft, and leave time for feedback and revisions.

evidence.quote: Assignments included a lot of tasks from the AI project of Berkeley CS 188, which can be found here:

themes.label: Reading, writing and presentations
themes.selection: If you are taking other courses with substantial reading or presentations, compare their deadlines before finalising your course combination.
themes.study: Note the arguments and evidence as you read. Outline essays and presentations first, then check clarity and citations.

themes.label: Programming and debugging
themes.selection: If you have limited programming experience, allow time for writing and debugging code when planning your workload.
themes.study: Run and modify examples yourself, write small tests for your programs, and keep notes on debugging.

evidence.quote: The programming questions are easier, and you can find most of them (those from Berkeley CS 188) on GitHub, so you can check your output before submission.
In tutorial, TA will teach you how to apply what you learn, including implementing them in Python.

themes.label: Practice and revision
themes.selection: If you learn best through regular practice, compare the study methods and time commitments described in the reviews.
themes.study: Review mistakes and key concepts each week. Attempt problems independently, then try different question types to check your understanding.

evidence.quote: The exams are not difficult and extremely similar to past papers (go to your senior friends and find more, since he will only provide one sample), so you can get familiar with the questions with very little preparations before exams.
The past papers are mostly useless due to change in syllabus.

themes.label: Class participation
themes.selection: Check the current participation and attendance requirements. Experiences from previous semesters may not reflect this semester's rules.
themes.study: Confirm participation marks and attendance rules at the start, and add class activities and submission deadlines to your calendar.

evidence.quote: When I sit in the classroom the classmates kept asking questions which is good for their own understanding and the course participation level.
I ticked "attendance", but there is no attendance in the course.

themes.label: Group work

themes.study: Agree on responsibilities, deadlines, and checkpoints at the start. Check progress together regularly.

evidence.quote: 6-7 individual assignments which is easy to finish, and a final group project with a group report.
Short assignments every couple of weeks, with one group project with a presentation and a report at the end of the semester.

sections.content:
Take COMP2211 or COMP4211 instead.

Old school AI contents. It should more related to algorithm not AI.
-Simple intelligent agents (designing agent controller by rules, supervised learning, genetic programming)
-Search (Uniformed, Heuristic, Adversarial, MDP)
-Learning (supervised, unsupervised, reinforcement, rule-based)
-Knowledge Representation, Reasoning, and Planning
-Multi-agent systems,  game theory and auction
-Uncertainty
Personally think he MDP and reinforcement learning are very useful and practical. Others is either old school AI algorithms.
The alpha beta pruning is exactly same as that in COMP2211.
The last two weeks covered logics, which is highly overlapped with contents of COMP2711.

Except for MDP and reinforcement learning, other contents are not useful now. Also the programming is not abundant. Please take COMP2211 or COMP4211 instead, they are much more fruitful and practical.

Only if you are interested in AI like me, you can find contents interesting.

The main reason for me to take this course is I looked at Huiru's Github and found her photo is very beautiful, I want to get attention from beautiful woman, ahahahahahaha.

Once I even ask about out-of syllabus questions (Whether parameters in reinforcement learning is biased or not?) she can still answer, this is very strong, this is very rare and fully demonstrate how strong Huiru is. 🛐

Huiru is very beautiful, her smile is very curing. She is younger and much prettier than her photos. My fellow classmates are very active and sometimes ask funny questions. Thank you miss Huiru for giving me energetic mornings in my last semester.

He asked Huiru for more exercises and past paper questions and he covered those in tutorials. Once I appeal "sympathy" marks in midterm because I count 2 blanks less, he is very funny and tell me that he is very nice and already given.

Also PGTA Yunhao and Jinhui teach good. Both can teach well and can answer our questions. Reliable TAs that I have seen in 3000+ courses.
But part of tutorials are not useful for exams. Can take those as reference.
sections.grading:
Same as COMP2211, the boss is Huiru. At the very beginning she is IA in COMP2211 when she graduated PhD and fully follows the grading scheme from Desmond.

Personally thinking: The chance for getting good grade is more than that in COMP2211, but higher chance to getting fried in Exams.
The exams of COMP2211 is very DIFFICULT, you need to have very deep thinking and analysis. Like analyse the algorithm have which impact or in which case will be failed to get good. In this semester COMP2211 final exam they made questions like giving you new loss function and analyse the performance. In my semester they even ask me to rewrite 4 NESTED FOR LOOPS WITHOUT ANY LOOPS!!! I totally GGed. Those are Desmond's idea
聽我說謝謝你，因為有你，溫暖了四季, because he want all of us to have very deep learning in AI. But COMP2211 is much more fruitful than this. Also Desmond released limited past paper and he and Huiru design exams with totally different (difficult) questions.

But in COMP3211 Huiru mostly design dry run(execute program with given inputs) questions, which very similar with past paper. She also releases many past papers and prefers to teaches many examples in lectures. So this is more "easier" to get high score in exams. sections.content:
I don't understand what is the emphasis of this course.

In the beginning, she introduced stimulus-response agents and state machine. Then, it was about graph search and reinforcement learning. After the midterm, the topic becomes game theory and auction. More fantastically, she further introduced logical representation and conditional probability in the last two lectures.

Now, I think you can observe the problem: Most of the knowledge appeared in this course is covered in other courses. For example, stimulus-response agents and state machine in ELEC1100 Final Project, graph search in COMP 3711H, logical representation in COMP 2711, conditional probability in MATH 2421.

Because COMP 3211 covers so many contents, it cannot dig into one topic very much. And the result is: you have only learned a lot of superficial knowledge, but you don't understand the real principle and usage.

So, I think it's not worth spending your time on these overlapped and superficial knowledge. You should spend your time on some meaningful things.

sections.grading:
It's good. around full marks for assignment & ~1SD above mean in exam is A
midterm is much harder than final in my opinion, final has some dry-run problems, format is similar to the past papers given. my way of revising is to do the past papers and note down which questions i got wrong, then do those questions again until i can get them right. then 1 day before the exam re-do all the past papers given from start to finish, this can give you fresher memories on the questions before the exam as the exam has very similar format to ppq. also do all the examples in lecture notes, assignments and tutorials, make sure you understand how to do them

below are some strategies i found useful for some frequently appearing exam questions, these exam questions are quite important make sure you can understand them well, when you're out of ideas for similar questions, try to think back on these strategies to see if they can help:
- how to prove an SR agent CANNOT do a boundary follow task?
    1.usually due to the perceptual aliasing problem:
        1. place the robot at the boundary
        2. place the robot at another position of a boundary, with the **same sensor readings**
        3. apply the **production system rules**
        4. show robot at these 2 positions must take **different actions**

- how to formulate auctions as non-bayesian games?
    1. N, A is trivial usually
    2. U:
        1. consider these 5 cases below, with their sub-cases linked to **special conditions** e.g. special tie-breaking conditions, reserved price. Need to enumerate on the sub-case i.e. bid profile: e.g. bid profile = (2, 0, 1), agent 1 is unique extremum(highest), agent 2 is lowest, agent 3 is in the middle. Consider what would happen to this sub case, if the bid profile is (2,0,1), what would the utility be under any special conditions e.g. special tie breaking rules
        2. an arbitrary agent i is unique extremum(highest/lowest)
        3. agent i ties with some others for extremum, but not all ties
        4. all equal
        5. agent i is not extremum, unique extremum is among others
        6. agent i is not extremum, extremum ties among others
  - example ppq: 25 final Q5, 23 final Q9

- how to find all NE in a formulated non-bayesian auction?
    1. highly correlated with the method above, it's like a dry-run of the above method after you finished the above method. for each case in utility func, enumerate all possible **sub-cases**
    2. then enumerate over all agents in each **sub-case**
            - e.g. one sub-case in util func is: (2, 0, 1), enumerate over 2, 0 and 1 where each of these 3 is an agent's bid. Will this bid be an NE according to the rules in question?
    3. if one agent can get higher util ⇒ not NE; if none ⇒ NE

- which of the following MUST BE a NE in auction?
    
   [see attachment 1.png]
    
    1. a < b ⇒ 1 - a > 1 - b. But we don’t know if (1-a)/2 > 1-b or not, it depends on the values of a and b!
    2. consider 1st column
        1. for player 1, it’s unknown whether (1-a)/2 > 1-b or not
    3. consider 2nd column:
        1. for player 1, (1 - b)/2 must be > 0, so circle this number in the btm right cell
    4. consider the 1st row:
        1. for player 2, it’s unknown whether (1-a)/2 > 1-b or not
    5. consider the 2nd row:
        1. for player 2, (1 - b)/2 must be > 0, so circle this number in the btm right cell
    6. thus btm right cell is overlapped, thus it’s an NE

- why does the cell (a, b) / (b, a) MUST NOT be an NE?
    
    [see attachment 1.png]
    
    1. if (a, b) is NE: 0 ≥ (1 - b)/2 ⇒ 0 ≥ 1 - b ⇒ b ≥ 1 ⇒ b = 1 due to the “suppose in general…” constraint
    2. if (a, b) is NE: 1 - b ≥ (1 - a)/2 ⇒ as b = 1 ⇒ 0 ≥ (1-a)/2 ⇒ 0 ≥ 1 - a ⇒ a ≥ 1 ⇒ a = 1 due to the “suppose in general…” constraint
    3. now a = b = 1, but the “suppose in general…” constraint says that a < b, so there’s a contradiction!
        
        [see attachment 2.png]

- when is (a, a) below a NE? Thus given (b, b) is the ONLY POSSIBLE other NE, when will (b, b) be the ONLY NE?
    
    [see attachment 1.png]
    
    1. when (1 - a)/2 ≥ 1 - b (by maximizing u1 and u2 on row and col)
    2. when (1 - a)/2 < 1 - b

- in the general case of first price auction below, why is (am, …, am) ALWAYS an NE?
    
    [see attachment 3.png]
    
    1. consider a representative player j
    2. all other players’ actions are all am ⇒ profile sj = (am, …, am)
    3. thus you’re tie breaking now: uj(sj, am) = 1/n * (1-am) ≥ 0 according to the “in general, suppose…” assumption
    4. now if player j does not take am, but take a smaller-valued action ak
    5. then it cannot win the auction as there will be other players(actually all other players) bidding a bigger price ⇒ j's util becomes 0
    
    [see attachment 4.png]

- when will (ai, …, ai) be an NE below in the general case for 1st price auction?
    
    [see attachment 3.png]
    
    [see attachment 5.png]
    
    1. case 2 is the best response iff its util is larger than case 3
    2. (the neon yellow words are the part after “iff” for the (ai, …, ai) case in the lecture notes screenshot

- when will (x1, …, xn) with largest item ai occurring k times be an NE below in the general case for 1st price auction?
    
    [see attachment 3.png]
    
    [see attachment 6.png]
    
    [see attachment 7.png]

The lecture slides are not bad, and his teaching is average reading slides level, with minimal extra elaboration. Also, if you ask questions during class, he has a high chance to misinterpret your question, and will answer irrelevant stuff, so it is better for you to ask questions after class such that you have more time to state your question clearly.

That being said, he is still a nice person, and he answers emails quite quickly.
sections.grading:
3 assignments: 20%
Midterm: 25% (Everything up to local search)
Final: 55% (Everything up to logic)
Mean/Low/LQ/Median/UQ/High:
A1: 98.25/79/99/99.75/100/100
A2: 95.28/0/98/100/100/100
A3: 95.06/49/95/99/99/100
Midterm: 80.95/49/74/85/90/99
Final: 73.12/39.5/62.31/76.5/85.25/96.5

The assignments are mostly trivial and poorly designed. I have disagreements with one of the solutions in the assignment and tried to argue with the TA through email, and the TA seems to have trouble understanding English and just did not answer after a few turns of 雞同鴨講 discussions.

Also, the assignment solutions are released very late (within one week before final exam) and are only released because I urge the professor to do so. The scores for assignment 2 are released after the final exam scores, which shows the incompetence of the TAs.

Since the assignments and midterm are too easy (mean = 80 is even higher than my COMP3511 open-book midterm in previous semester), the final is made slightly more difficult, but the overall scores are still very high, so you really need to be careful when doing the exams. The exams need you to recite the algorithms in order to run them for a few iterations on paper. You also need the update rules for the reinforcement learning part, so please recite them as well. Very few COMP2211 type theoretical questions are asked in the exams. No sample papers are provided, and the sample questions are too few (2 questions each for each exam) and too simple, so please don't trust your exam will be that simple.

sections.content: The course provides an overview of AI fundamentals, focusing on how algorithms work at a conceptual level. While it covers the basics, the explanations often lack depth and are overly simplistic, presented in a "calculator-style" manner. There’s no emphasis on coding or practical implementation, which makes it feel incomplete for students hoping to gain hands-on experience. Additionally, the course doesn’t include any engaging or creative projects, which could have been a great way to apply the concepts learned. The exam is straightforward and calculation-heavy, but without much variety or real-world relevance.
sections.teaching: Lectures rely entirely on PowerPoint slides, and attending them feels optional since everything is already on the slides. If you choose to go, you’ll likely find a small group of attendees.
sections.grading: The grading system is fair, but the high class average makes it challenging to score well. With the mean often around 70, this translates to a C
sections.workload: The workload is light, with only three assignments throughout the semester. Each assignment can be completed in two days or less if you have a basic understanding of machine learning concepts. While not particularly challenging, they do require some thought and a clear understanding of the algorithms discussed in class. Overall, the workload is manageable and doesn’t demand much time or effort.

sections.content:
These are the brief content for this semester. Not very difficult things, but take time to remember to digest.
But most of the things seem not that related to AI... The course name is better viewed as "COMP 3211 - Fundamental things BEFORE you learn AI"
You can have a look at them and decide whether you are into those things:

1. Simple Intelligent Agents
    Designing Agent Controller by Rules: Programming agents (like a thermostat or a simple game bot) using specific rules it must follow. For example, "if the room temperature is below 20°C, turn on the heater."
    Supervised Learning: Teach an agent by giving it examples. Each example has inputs and the correct output (like teaching a child with flashcards). Over time, the agent learns to predict the output from the inputs.
    Genetic Programming: Create programs or agents automatically by mimicking the process of natural evolution. Programs evolve over generations to become more effective at performing tasks.

2. Search
    Uninformed Search: Do not have any extra information about the states beyond what’s provided in the problem definition. It blindly searches for the solution (like looking for an object in a dark room).
   Heuristic Search: Using clever guesswork, to make searches more efficient (like playing "hot and cold" to find an object).
    Adversarial Search: Used in scenarios like chess, where you have an opponent. The goal is to find the best move considering the opponent will also be trying to outsmart you.
    MDP (Markov Decision Processes): A mathematical framework for modeling decision-making where outcomes are partly random and partly under the control of a decision-maker.

3. Learning
    Supervised Learning: As mentioned, this involves learning from labeled data—data that has the answer key.
    Unsupervised Learning: Here, you work with data without labels. The goal might be to identify patterns or groupings in the data.
    Reinforcement Learning: Learning based on feedback—it’s about taking actions in an environment to maximize some notion of cumulative reward.
    Rule-based Learning: This involves learning the rules that govern a system from examples or through direct programming of rules.

4. Knowledge Representation, Reasoning, and Planning
    Knowledge Representation: How to store knowledge in a computer so it can be used efficiently.
    Reasoning: Deals with using the stored knowledge to answer questions or solve problems.
    Planning: Involves creating a series of actions to achieve a specific goal, like planning a route for a robot to follow.

5. Multi-agent Systems, Game Theory, and Auction
    Multi-agent Systems: Systems composed of multiple interacting agents. They can cooperate, coordinate, or compete with each other.
    Game Theory: The study of mathematical models of conflict and cooperation between intelligent rational decision-makers.
    Auction Theory: Design and analysis of auction mechanisms, focusing on how goods or services are allocated and at what prices.

6. Uncertainty
    Situations where it's impossible to know exactly what will happen. AI systems, like humans, often make decisions under uncertainty. Techniques like probability and statistics are used to handle uncertainty in AI.

sections.content:
Dekai's interest lie in natural language processing, and that really shows in this class. A ton of AI techniques are introduced, but they are usually in the context of translation or processing languages. People that have taken the course have probably heard "Time flies like an arrow" or "Fruit flies like an apple" a billion times. (BTW in case "fruit flies like an apple" doesn't make sense to you, a fruit fly is a type of fly.) There is also some random Chinese thrown in there sometimes, but it's not strictly necessary to know it to understand the class. It'll just increase enjoyment of the material somewhat.

There are two major topics in AI: searching/updating and knowledge representation. For searching/updating, you'll revise naïve search methods (BFS, DFS, Dijkstra's) and then be introduced to heurstic search, EM algorithms, forward backward algorithms, Knuth's algorithm, etc. For knowledge representation, you begin with hidden Markov models (HMMs) and then weighted finite state automata (WFSAs), unrolled HMMs and FSAs, progressing to AND/OR graphs and finite state grammars (FSGs). There is also a small taste of inversion transduction grammars.

Oh and because it's Dekai you also have Scheme thrown in there randomly in the beginning.
sections.teaching:
If you can't tell, I'm a big fan of Dekai's teaching style. He's really enthusiastic and is willing to force students to break that mold of "never asking questions" a lot. He will try his best to force you to speak in his class. His classes have a sort of "American" atmosphere to them, if that makes sense.

He also loves going on tangents related to his research, and he loves functional programming and cool things. He also makes use of the whiteboard a lot, which really beats the "reading the powerpoint" professors. I'm sure you know which ones I'm talking about.
sections.grading:
I ticked "attendance", but there is no attendance in the course. However, if you don't attend class, you'll be 100% screwed for the midterm and final simply because the notes are not going to be online and are only given when the topic is fully covered. He also does examples on the whiteboard, which are NOT in the notes, and he will test you on them.

There are also a bunch of other smaller assignments that apply what are taught in class. Those are not very difficult and can be done in about 30 minutes.

I didn't study for the midterm outside of just doing the assignments and taking notes in class and got a really decent grade, so the midterm is not very hard. The final exam is open handwritten notes, and since I took notes for every class I did really well. There was a scheme question at the end, but since almost everyone forgot their scheme they were just given marks for attempting it.

The distribution of grades is standard Dekai:
Midterm exam: ~20%
Final exam: ~25%
Participation: ~5%
Assignments: ~50%

Since it's Dekai, you have his typical marking scheme, which is a curve with the following guarantee:
> 85% is at LEAST an A
> 75% is at LEAST a B
> 65% is at LEAST a C
> 55% is at LEAST a D
sections.workload:
There was one programming assignment that was really easy if you knew a small amount of Scheme. The other homework is written and really easy. I think pretty much everyone just got those marks for free as long as your answer makes some sort of sense.

As long as you don't mind attending every lesson and copying diagrams on the board while listening to really awesome material about AI the workload is really light. No need to study very much for either the midterm or the final. The homeworks are easily completable within 30 minutes, and there are not that many.
